title: Palmer Luckey Calls H-1B Lobby Defense a Sham, Defenders Push Back
excerpt: The Anduril founder says lobbyists defend a program widely used to undercut American wages and that silent executives know it. H-1B supporters, from Paul Graham to university leaders, say the alternative to a global hire is often a job exported abroad.
body:
• Anduril founder Palmer Luckey has attacked the defense of the H-1B program by lobbyists as a sham, arguing many visas replace American workers with cheaper labor rather than fill rare-skill gaps.
  • Luckey backed Vice President JD Vance's figures that H-1B workers earn about $20,000 less than Americans in comparable jobs, and $48,000 less when hired through foreign outsourcing firms.
  • Defenders, including Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham, counter that the most qualified person should get the job and that blocking a hire often exports the job abroad instead.
  • For Indian H-1B holders and applicants: Luckey is an employer voice, not a policymaker — his remarks change no rule, but signal growing employer-side support for wage-based reforms and the $100,000 petition fee.

Palmer Luckey, founder of Oculus VR and co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, has called the lobbying defense of the H-1B visa program a sham, arguing that staffing agencies and technology companies use the program to replace American workers with cheaper labor. His remarks, responding to Vice President JD Vance, come from inside the industry that hires most heavily through the program, and Luckey says he supports bringing exceptional talent to the United States.

"Immigration policy must be driven by the present, not the past," Luckey wrote, according to A Curious Loyalist's summary of his posts. Pointing to exceptional entrepreneurs who arrived decades ago, he argued, does little to answer concerns about hiring practices today.

Luckey's Case: Replacement, Not Recruitment

Luckey's argument has three parts. First, recruiting scarce talent and cutting payroll are different objectives, and too much H-1B hiring, he says, is the second dressed up as the first. Second, abuse destroys public trust: companies exploiting the system undermine political support for legitimate recruitment from abroad. Third, industry silence is deliberate — executives who privately agree fear criticism from the right over displaced workers and accusations of prejudice from the left.

https://x.com/FortuneMagazine/status/2113676939038798309

"I know too many tech execs in particular who feel trapped, like the only winning move is to stay silent."

— Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries

The flash point was Vance's October 8 news conference. Vance claimed H-1B workers earn $20,000 less than American citizens in comparable positions, with the gap reaching $48,000 for workers brought in through foreign outsourcing firms — figures Luckey endorsed. American Conservatives reported Luckey's view that a worker doing routine web design for half an American counterpart's pay does not meet the program's stated purpose.

The Counter-Argument From H-1B Defenders

Defenders reject the displacement framing. Y Combinator co-founder Paul Graham's position, at the center of a widely discussed exchange with Luckey analyzed by Pirate Wires, is straightforward: "I believe the most qualified person should get the job." In that debate, Y Combinator partner Ankit Gupta argued the choice is often not between a foreign worker and an American worker at all. "The counterfactual is that job opening getting exported to Shenzhen, Shanghai, Bangalore, Toronto, or London," Gupta wrote — if the hire cannot happen in the United States, the role leaves the country entirely.

Universities make a related case. The UC San Diego guidance on H-1B sponsorship describes the category as reserved for specialty occupations requiring highly specialized knowledge and at least a bachelor's degree in a directly related field, and advocates quoted by Inside Higher Ed say campuses depend on it for niche expertise in science, engineering and medicine.

Defenders also note the program's guardrails. As the Berkeley International Office explains, most private-sector petitions are subject to the annual cap and lottery, while universities and nonprofit research organizations are cap-exempt, and employers must meet required-wage obligations. On that view, the problem is enforcement against bad actors, not the program itself.

Where the Two Sides Differ

The dispute is narrower than the rhetoric suggests. Luckey does not call for ending skilled immigration, and Graham does not defend fraud. They differ on the typical case: Luckey says it is a replaceable worker brought in on price; defenders say it is a scarce specialist.

That distinction matters for policy now in motion: a $100,000 fee on many new petitions, Florida and Texas university pauses, and proposed wage-weighted selection. If hiring falls mainly among lower-paid outsourcing placements, Luckey's account gains support; if labs, hospitals and startups report unfilled specialist roles or work moving abroad, the defenders' account does.

What This Means for Indian Professionals

Indian nationals receive the largest share of H-1B visas, so a debate led by a prominent employer carries weight even though Luckey holds no office. Nothing in his remarks changes eligibility, the lottery, or a current holder's status. What it signals is that support for reform is coming from employers as well as politicians. Readers should weigh the concrete rules that do apply — the petition fee, wage obligations, and state university pauses — over the exchange itself.
